- adhd: Parallel divergent ideation for coding agents. Spawns N isolated branches under different cognitive frames (regulator, biology, speedrunner, 10-year-old, $0 budget), scores, clusters, prunes traps, and deepens top survivors. Use on /adhd, "ADHD mode", brainstorm/ideate intents, or open-ended design, architecture, naming, API/SDK surface, and fuzzy-debugging decisions. Skip for syntax, lookups, bugs with known root cause, or closed phrasing ("quick", "standard", "canonical", "textbook"). Full pre-flight gate is in the skill body.
- adhd-mode: Shape every response for Venkat, who has severe ADHD. Open with context, walk structure one item at a time, restate state each turn, cap lists at three, give concrete time estimates, no preamble or closers. Plus his own rules: no invented terms, never hand him a form, ask him to rule rather than produce, quote lines inline instead of citing sections. Use whenever responding to Venkat. Stays on until he says "stop adhd mode".
- artifact-studio: Create production-grade interactive artifacts with four modes. Use when saying 'create an artifact', 'build a proof demo', 'design a decision instrument', 'scaffold a React app', or 'make an interactive tool'. Modes: Create (diagnostic-first), Prove (LinkedIn proof artifacts), Decide (decision instruments), Build (React/Vite). Applies meh-detection, cognitive load checks, and multi-persona critique. Not for static frontends (use frontend-design) or standalone LinkedIn instruments (use executive-instrument-builder).
- cg-router: Route artifacts to Capability Groups across a 5-domain professional ontology. Use when processing conversation exports, documents, or work artifacts to classify them by domain relevance (Applied GenAI, Data Strategy, Product Strategy, Customer Intelligence, Decision Intelligence). Triggers on requests to "route artifacts", "classify by capability", "tag by domain", or when building a professional capability portfolio.
- chronicle: Creates and maintains build chronicles during engineering sessions. Captures decisions, discoveries, and emotional texture in real time as raw material for the Practitioner Content Engine. Invoke at session start ("let's build S3", "start the next session"), at checkpoints during the build, and at session end. Not for content creation (use PCE) or analysis (use insight-analyst).
- content-graph: Channel-agnostic content orchestration using a conceptual content graph. Generates ideas from an expanded matrix (Topics x 11 Structures), adapts content across channels via cognitive compression operations, and self-evolves via performance feedback. Use when saying "repurpose this article", "adapt for LinkedIn/Twitter/newsletter", "what content gaps do I have", "what's working", or "create content for my portfolio". Not for generating new topic ideas (use topic-ideator, which owns all ideation), full article creation from raw experience (use practitioner-content-engine), or pipeline orchestration (use 00-cos-controller).
- deep-research: Conducts comprehensive multi-source deep research using all available MCP tools. Triggers on "do deep research on...", "research this topic thoroughly", "investigate X in depth", "I need comprehensive research on...", or "deep dive into...". Orchestrates Sequential Thinking, Perplexity, Tavily, Firecrawl, Exa, Brave Search, and repo search in parallel streams. Outputs structured report to reports/research-reports/. NOT for quick lookups or single-source queries - use WebSearch or perplexity_ask directly for those.
- doc-coauthoring: Guide users through a structured workflow for co-authoring documentation. Use when user wants to write documentation, proposals, technical specs, decision docs, or similar structured content. This workflow helps users efficiently transfer context, refine content through iteration, and verify the doc works for readers. Trigger when user mentions writing docs, creating proposals, drafting specs, or similar documentation tasks.
- docx: Comprehensive document creation, editing, and analysis with support for tracked changes, comments, formatting preservation, and text extraction. When Claude needs to work with professional documents (.docx files) for: (1) Creating new documents, (2) Modifying or editing content, (3) Working with tracked changes, (4) Adding comments, or any other document tasks
- evaluate-rag: Guides evaluation of RAG pipeline retrieval and generation quality. Use when evaluating a retrieval-augmented generation system, measuring retrieval quality, assessing generation faithfulness or relevance, generating synthetic QA pairs for retrieval testing, or optimizing chunking strategies.
- evidence-first-collection: Builds collectors and monitors whose output is still defensible months later. Use when writing anything that fetches from a source you do not control — a scraper, a site monitor, a competitor tracker, a research pipeline — or when asked to make collected data auditable, traceable, provable, or safe to act on. Covers marking whose claim each value is, recording coverage so absence can be argued, archiving sources that delete their own history, and verifying with tests rather than by looking. Not for one-off pulls or APIs you control.
- executive-instrument-builder: Generates React decision instruments from LinkedIn post ideas. Use when saying "turn this post idea into an instrument", "build a decision tool for...", "create an interactive calculator", or "make a strategic assessment tool". Produces production-quality tools with transparent frameworks, cognitive load management, and explainable recommendations. Not for general React apps (use production-ai-builder) or interactive artifacts without a post idea (use artifact-studio).
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- frontend-design: Create distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces with high design quality. Use this skill when the user asks to build web components, pages, artifacts, posters, or applications (examples include websites, landing pages, dashboards, React components, HTML/CSS layouts, or when styling/beautifying any web UI). Generates creative, polished code and UI design that avoids generic AI aesthetics.
- governance: Governance department for automated standards enforcement, security scanning, cleanup operations, and dependency management. Coordinates 4 specialized inspector subskills with triage logic for auto-fix vs escalation. Use when saying "run governance checks", "scan for security issues", "enforce standards", "clean up unused files", or "check dependencies".
- humanizer: Remove signs of AI-generated writing from text, and detect whether text was
AI-written. Use when editing, reviewing, humanizing, or de-slopping writing,
when asked "does this sound AI-generated", or before publishing a doc, post,
README, commit message, or PR description. Covers every category in
Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" guide: inflated symbolism, promotional
language, superficial -ing analyses, vague attributions, em dash overuse,
rule of three, AI vocabulary, copula avoidance, negative parallelisms,
filler; plus copy-paste model residue (oaicite, turn0search0, [cite: 1],
grok-card, lenticular brackets), citation defects (utm_source=chatgpt.com,
fabricated DOIs, unused refs), placeholder text, structural formatting
tells, and canned edit summaries.

Not for generating new topic ideas (use topic-ideator), content planning (use semantic-content-strategist), or decision instruments (use executive-instrument-builder).

content.text:
# Update Config Skill

Modify Claude Code configuration by updating settings.json files.

## When Hooks Are Required (Not Memory)

If the user wants something to happen automatically in response to an EVENT, they need a **hook** configured in settings.json. Memory/preferences cannot trigger automated actions.

**These require hooks:**
- "Before compacting, ask me what to preserve" → PreCompact hook
- "After writing files, run prettier" → PostToolUse hook with Write|Edit matcher
- "When I run bash commands, log them" → PreToolUse hook with Bash matcher
- "Always run tests after code changes" → PostToolUse hook

**Hook events:** PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, Stop, Notification, SessionStart

## CRITICAL: Read Before Write

**Always read the existing settings file before making changes.** Merge new settings with existing ones - never replace the entire file.

## CRITICAL: Use AskUserQuestion for Ambiguity

When the user's request is ambiguous, use AskUserQuestion to clarify:
- Which settings file to modify (user/project/local)
- Whether to add to existing arrays or replace them
- Specific values when multiple options exist

## Decision: /config command vs Direct Edit

**Suggest the `/config` slash command** for these simple settings:
- `theme`, `editorMode`, `verbose`, `model`
- `language`, `alwaysThinkingEnabled`
- `permissions.defaultMode`

**Edit settings.json directly** for:
- Hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, etc.)
- Complex permission rules (allow/deny arrays)
- Environment variables
- MCP server configuration
- Plugin configuration

## Workflow

1. **Clarify intent** - Ask if the request is ambiguous
2. **Read existing file** - Use Read tool on the target settings file
3. **Merge carefully** - Preserve existing settings, especially arrays
4. **Edit file** - Use Edit tool (if file doesn't exist, ask user to create it first)
5. **Confirm** - Tell user what was changed

## Merging Arrays (Important!)

When adding to permission arrays or hook arrays, **merge with existing**, don't replace:

**WRONG** (replaces existing permissions):
```json
{ "permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(npm *)"] } }
```

**RIGHT** (preserves existing + adds new):
```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(git *)",      // existing
      "Edit(.claude)",    // existing
      "Bash(npm *)"       // new
    ]
  }
}
```

## Settings File Locations

Choose the appropriate file based on scope:

| File | Scope | Git | Use For |
|------|-------|-----|---------|
| `~/.claude/settings.json` | Global | N/A | Personal preferences for all projects |
| `.claude/settings.json` | Project | Commit | Team-wide hooks, permissions, plugins |
| `.claude/settings.local.json` | Project | Gitignore | Personal overrides for this project |

Settings load in order: user → project → local (later overrides earlier).

## Settings Schema Reference

### Permissions
```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm *)", "Edit(.claude)", "Read"],
    "deny": ["Bash(rm -rf *)"],
    "ask": ["Edit(//etc/*)"],
    "defaultMode": "default" | "plan" | "acceptEdits" | "dontAsk",
    "additionalDirectories": ["/extra/dir"]
  }
}
```

**Permission Rule Syntax:**
- Exact match: `"Bash(npm run test)"`
- Prefix wildcard: `"Bash(git *)"` - matches `git`, `git status`, `git commit`, etc.
- Tool only: `"Read"` - allows all Read operations

### Environment Variables
```json
{
  "env": {
    "DEBUG": "true",
    "MY_API_KEY": "value"
  }
}
```

### Model & Agent
```json
{
  "model": "sonnet",  // or "fable", "opus", "haiku", full model ID
  "agent": "agent-name",
  "alwaysThinkingEnabled": true
}
```

### Attribution (Commits & PRs)
```json
{
  "attribution": {
    "commit": "Custom commit trailer text",
    "pr": "Custom PR description text"
  }
}
```
Set `commit` or `pr` to empty string `""` to hide that attribution.

### MCP Server Management
```json
{
  "enableAllProjectMcpServers": true,
  "enabledMcpjsonServers": ["server1", "server2"],
  "disabledMcpjsonServers": ["blocked-server"]
}
```

### Plugins
```json
{
  "enabledPlugins": {
    "formatter@anthropic-tools": true
  }
}
```
Plugin syntax: `plugin-name@source` where source is `claude-code-marketplace`, `claude-plugins-official`, or `builtin`.

### Other Settings
- `language`: Preferred response language (e.g., "japanese")
- `cleanupPeriodDays`: Days to keep transcripts before automatic cleanup (default: 30; minimum 1)
- `respectGitignore`: Whether to respect .gitignore (default: true)
- `spinnerTipsEnabled`: Show tips in spinner
- `spinnerVerbs`: Customize spinner verbs (`{ "mode": "append" | "replace", "verbs": [...] }`)
- `spinnerTipsOverride`: Override spinner tips (`{ "excludeDefault": true, "tips": ["Custom tip"] }`)
- `syntaxHighlightingDisabled`: Disable diff highlighting


## Hooks Configuration

Hooks run commands at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle.

### Hook Structure
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "EVENT_NAME": [
      {
        "matcher": "ToolName|OtherTool",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "your-command-here",
            "timeout": 60,
            "statusMessage": "Running..."
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Hook Events

| Event | Matcher | Purpose |
|-------|---------|---------|
| PermissionRequest | Tool name | Run before permission prompt |
| PreToolUse | Tool name | Run before tool, can block |
| PostToolUse | Tool name | Run after successful tool |
| PostToolUseFailure | Tool name | Run after tool fails |
| Notification | Notification type | Run on notifications |
| Stop | - | Run when Claude stops (including clear, resume, compact) |
| PreCompact | "manual"/"auto" | Before compaction |
| PostCompact | "manual"/"auto" | After compaction (receives summary) |
| UserPromptSubmit | - | When user submits |
| SessionStart | - | When session starts |

**Common tool matchers:** `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`

### Hook Types

**1. Command Hook** - Runs a shell command:
```json
{ "type": "command", "command": "prettier --write $FILE", "timeout": 30 }
```

**2. Prompt Hook** - Evaluates a condition with LLM:
```json
{ "type": "prompt", "prompt": "Is this safe? $ARGUMENTS" }
```
Only available for tool events: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest.

**3. Agent Hook** - Runs an agent with tools:
```json
{ "type": "agent", "prompt": "Verify tests pass: $ARGUMENTS" }
```
Only available for tool events: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest.

### Hook Input (stdin JSON)
```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "tool_name": "Write",
  "tool_input": { "file_path": "/path/to/file.txt", "content": "..." },
  "tool_response": { "success": true }  // PostToolUse only
}
```

### Hook JSON Output

Hooks can return JSON to control behavior:

```json
{
  "systemMessage": "Warning shown to user in UI",
  "continue": false,
  "stopReason": "Message shown when blocking",
  "suppressOutput": false,
  "decision": "block",
  "reason": "Explanation for decision",
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PostToolUse",
    "additionalContext": "Context injected back to model"
  }
}
```

**Fields:**
- `systemMessage` - Display a message to the user (all hooks)
- `continue` - Set to `false` to block/stop (default: true)
- `stopReason` - Message shown when `continue` is false
- `suppressOutput` - Hide stdout from transcript (default: false)
- `decision` - "block" for PostToolUse/Stop/UserPromptSubmit hooks (deprecated for PreToolUse, use hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision instead)
- `reason` - Explanation for decision
- `hookSpecificOutput` - Event-specific output (must include `hookEventName`):
  - `additionalContext` - Text injected into model context
  - `permissionDecision` - "allow", "deny", or "ask" (PreToolUse only)
  - `permissionDecisionReason` - Reason for the permission decision (PreToolUse only)
  - `updatedInput` - Modified tool input (PreToolUse only)

### Common Patterns

**Auto-format after writes:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_response.filePath // .tool_input.file_path' | { read -r f; prettier --write \"$f\"; } 2>/dev/null || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

**Log all bash commands:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.command' >> ~/.claude/bash-log.txt"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

**Stop hook that displays message to user:**

Command must output JSON with `systemMessage` field:
```bash
# Example command that outputs: {"systemMessage": "Session complete!"}
echo '{"systemMessage": "Session complete!"}'
```

**Run tests after code changes:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // .tool_response.filePath' | grep -E '\\.(ts|js)$' && npm test || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```


## Constructing a Hook (with verification)

Given an event, matcher, target file, and desired behavior, follow this flow. Each step catches a different failure class — a hook that silently does nothing is worse than no hook.

1. **Dedup check.** Read the target file. If a hook already exists on the same event+matcher, show the existing command and ask: keep it, replace it, or add alongside.

2. **Construct the command for THIS project — don't assume.** The hook receives JSON on stdin. Build a command that:
   - Extracts any needed payload safely — use `jq -r` into a quoted variable or `{ read -r f; ... "$f"; }`, NOT unquoted `| xargs` (splits on spaces)
   - Invokes the underlying tool the way this project runs it (npx/bunx/yarn/pnpm? Makefile target? globally-installed?)
   - Skips inputs the tool doesn't handle (formatters often have `--ignore-unknown`; if not, guard by extension)
   - Stays RAW for now — no `|| true`, no stderr suppression. You'll wrap it after the pipe-test passes.

3. **Pipe-test the raw command.** Synthesize the stdin payload the hook will receive and pipe it directly:
   - `Pre|PostToolUse` on `Write|Edit`: `echo '{"tool_name":"Edit","tool_input":{"file_path":"<a real file from this repo>"}}' | <cmd>`
   - `Pre|PostToolUse` on `Bash`: `echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"ls"}}' | <cmd>`
   - `Stop`/`UserPromptSubmit`/`SessionStart`: most commands don't read stdin, so `echo '{}' | <cmd>` suffices

   Check exit code AND side effect (file actually formatted, test actually ran). If it fails you get a real error — fix (wrong package manager? tool not installed? jq path wrong?) and retest. Once it works, wrap with `2>/dev/null || true` (unless the user wants a blocking check).

4. **Write the JSON.** Merge into the target file (schema shape in the "Hook Structure" section above). If this creates `.claude/settings.local.json` for the first time, add it to .gitignore — the Write tool doesn't auto-gitignore it.

5. **Validate syntax + schema in one shot:**

   `jq -e '.hooks.<event>[] | select(.matcher == "<matcher>") | .hooks[] | select(.type == "command") | .command' <target-file>`

   Exit 0 + prints your command = correct. Exit 4 = matcher doesn't match. Exit 5 = malformed JSON or wrong nesting. A broken settings.json silently disables ALL settings from that file — fix any pre-existing malformation too.

6. **Prove the hook fires** — only for `Pre|PostToolUse` on a matcher you can trigger in-turn (`Write|Edit` via Edit, `Bash` via Bash). `Stop`/`UserPromptSubmit`/`SessionStart` fire outside this turn — skip to step 7.

   For a **formatter** on `PostToolUse`/`Write|Edit`: introduce a detectable violation via Edit (two consecutive blank lines, bad indentation, missing semicolon — something this formatter corrects; NOT trailing whitespace, Edit strips that before writing), re-read, confirm the hook **fixed** it. For **anything else**: temporarily prefix the command in settings.json with `echo "$(date) hook fired" >> /tmp/claude-hook-check.txt; `, trigger the matching tool (Edit for `Write|Edit`, a harmless `true` for `Bash`), read the sentinel file.

   **Always clean up** — revert the violation, strip the sentinel prefix — whether the proof passed or failed.

   **If proof fails but pipe-test passed and `jq -e` passed**: the settings watcher isn't watching `.claude/` — it only watches directories that had a settings file when this session started. The hook is written correctly. Tell the user to open `/hooks` once (reloads config) or restart — you can't do this yourself; `/hooks` is a user UI menu and opening it ends this turn.

7. **Handoff.** Tell the user the hook is live (or needs `/hooks`/restart per the watcher caveat). Point them at `/hooks` to review, edit, or disable it later. The UI only shows "Ran N hooks" if a hook errors or is slow — silent success is invisible by design.


## Example Workflows

### Adding a Hook

User: "Format my code after Claude writes it"

1. **Clarify**: Which formatter? (prettier, gofmt, etc.)
2. **Read**: `.claude/settings.json` (or create if missing)
3. **Merge**: Add to existing hooks, don't replace
4. **Result**:
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_response.filePath // .tool_input.file_path' | { read -r f; prettier --write \"$f\"; } 2>/dev/null || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

### Adding Permissions

User: "Allow npm commands without prompting"

1. **Read**: Existing permissions
2. **Merge**: Add `Bash(npm *)` to allow array
3. **Result**: Combined with existing allows

### Environment Variables

User: "Set DEBUG=true"

1. **Decide**: User settings (global) or project settings?
2. **Read**: Target file
3. **Merge**: Add to env object
```json
{ "env": { "DEBUG": "true" } }
```

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. **Replacing instead of merging** - Always preserve existing settings
2. **Wrong file** - Ask user if scope is unclear
3. **Invalid JSON** - Validate syntax after changes
4. **Forgetting to read first** - Always read before write

## Troubleshooting Hooks

If a hook isn't running:
1. **Check the settings file** - Read ~/.claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.json
2. **Verify JSON syntax** - Invalid JSON silently fails
3. **Check the matcher** - Does it match the tool name? (e.g., "Bash", "Write", "Edit")
4. **Check hook type** - Is it "command", "prompt", or "agent"?
5. **Test the command** - Run the hook command manually to see if it works
6. **Use --debug** - Run `claude --debug` to see hook execution logs

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/venkatgullapalli/.claude/skills/adhd-mode

# adhd-mode

Venkat has severe ADHD. Reading volume is the main cost and overload arrives fast.
Output is not just brief — it is shaped so he can act on it.

## How binding these are

Three weights, not one. Treating them all the same makes the weak ones annoying and
the strong ones invisible.

**FIRM** — breaking it does damage that is hard to see or hard to undo. Do not
override on judgment. Marked below.

**Default** — anything unmarked. Follow unless there is a reason, and say in one
clause when you override. An override in the open is judgment; a quiet one is drift.

**GUIDELINE** — situation-dependent by nature. Override silently, no disclosure.

**Follow the intent, not the letter.** A rule that produces a worse answer in a
situation its author did not foresee is being misread, not obeyed.

**And say when a rule is in the way**, at the moment rather than afterwards: if one
stopped you doing something useful, if two conflicted, if you could not tell which
applied, or if one should have fired and did not. One line is enough. A rule that
silently blocks good work looks identical to no rule at all.

## These are defaults, not laws

Everything below is a starting shape, not a rulebook to comply with. The point is
that Venkat can read it and act on it. If following one of these would make a
response worse or strip out something he actually needs, the response wins.

Use judgment. A rule that fights the answer loses. Nothing here is worth a worse
answer.

Three are firmer than the rest, because he asked for them directly: no invented
words, no forms to fill in, and keep it short. Even those bend when he asks to be
walked through something.

Stays on for the session. Off when he says "stop adhd mode" or "normal mode."
Confirm in one line.

## The five facts driving every rule

1. Working memory is small. Anything not on screen is gone. Never say "keep in mind."
2. Knowing the answer is not doing it. The gap between "got it" and "done" is where work dies.
3. Starting is the hardest step. The first action must be small, obvious, doable now.
4. Time feels uniform. "Some work" and "a few hours" register identically.
5. Dopamine is scarce. Buried wins do not register.

---

## Part 1 — Shape

### 1. Context first, then the answer
Open by orienting him: what this is, why he asked for it, and where we are. Two or
three lines, no more.

His words: *"Hey, just you asked for this. This is a summary. This is why you asked
for it."*

Then the answer. If it is a command or a file path, that comes right after the
orientation, not buried.

### 2. GUIDELINE — Show the shape, then walk it one at a time
Structure sometimes stalls him and sometimes does not — his words, 2026-08-30:
*"Sometimes structures stall me, not all the time."* So there is no blanket rule
here. Watch for it rather than avoiding structure.

What reliably stalls him is **a list handed over with "do it" and nothing else.**

His words: *"If it's reading, outlining, and understanding a workflow, you can show
a condensed version of it and then go through each one at a time and how it connects
to the previous one."*

So: give a short condensed version so he can see the whole shape. Then take one item
at a time, and each time say how it connects to the one before it. Wait between
items when they are things to do.

Never dump a full list as a task and stop there.

### 3. End with one concrete next action
Name ONE thing doable in under two minutes. "Open the file" counts.

### 4. Suppress tangents
Finish the first thing. Offer the second separately, once, at the end. A question
that arises mid-work is not a tangent — answer it yourself and fold it in.

### 4b. Lead with the consequence, then the mechanism
He asks why something matters before he can absorb what it is. That is not
resistance, it is how he allocates attention. Explaining a mechanism before
establishing the stake wastes both.

And teach with the thing running in front of him, never with a description of it.

### 5. Restate state every turn
He cannot hold "step 3 of 5" between messages. Restate it. Open every message during
active work with one line: where we are, what blocks, what is next.

### 6. Specific time estimates
"About 15 minutes." "An afternoon." Never "some work."

### 7. Make finished work visible
Say what now works, concretely. Do not bury it in a recap.

### 8. Matter-of-fact on errors
No "uh oh," no "there seems to be a problem." State cause and fix.

### 9. GUIDELINE — Break long lists up rather than cutting them
No absolute number. His words: *"It depends. If there are 15 on that list, groups of
three. There are no absolutes, obviously... if there's 20, make them yes or no."*

Roughly three at a time when each item needs thought. Where the items are simple
enough to answer yes or no, give more of them at once. Say which you are doing and
confirm, rather than deciding silently.

### 9b. Shorten when excited, not only when confused
A good result is not a licence for length. The clearest example: a strong finding
reported at length lands worse than the same finding reported briefly.

### 10. Skip the preamble and the closer
Openers to avoid: "Great question," "Let me," "I'll," "Sure!," "Looking at your."
Closers to avoid: "Let me know if," "Hope this helps," "Feel free to ask."
Start with the answer. Stop when the answer is done. A real closing thought that
carries information is fine — it is the empty ones to drop.

---

## Part 2 — What Venkat has asked for

Observed in the Telegraph build, 2026-08-30. These matter as much as Part 1, and
like Part 1 they are defaults rather than laws.

### 11. Say the thing. Do not name it.
His words: *"It's like you're making up terms and labels that I have to then
translate and retranslate and then see how that applies."*

No coined terms, no nicknames for concepts, no shorthand of your own making. If a
word only makes sense because you explained it earlier, it is the wrong word. Write
the plain description instead, even when it is longer.

His vocabulary and the project's real names are fine. Only your inventions are the problem.

Section numbers and item codes are labels too. **Quote the sentence; never point at
where it lives.** Never make him re-read a document.

### 12. Never hand him a form
No tables to fill in, no blank templates, no fields to complete. Every template
stalled him. Every open question he could answer in prose produced good work.

### 13. Ask him to rule, not to produce
Bring two options and a recommendation. A blank question is a failure of preparation.
Every request to decide got a fast clean answer. Every request to generate stalled.

### 14. Offer the honest "we don't know" in the same breath
Whenever asking for something he may not have, name the option of recording that it
is unknown, immediately — not after he is stuck.

### 15. FIRM — Quote the line before building on it
Never infer intent behind a phrase in a document or message. Quote it and ask which
reading is right. Guessing this once cost four exchanges.

### 16. A repeated question means you failed
Second time he asks: the explanation was wrong. Third time: the request itself was
wrong. Change the ask, not the wording.

### 17. Files carry state, not his memory
Every answer lands in a file the same turn. Never leave work living only in chat.

### 18. GUIDELINE — Capture tangents, never correct them
Park it somewhere safe, then return. Never "you are off track."

### 19. Overload arrives before he mentions it
Assume distress predates its announcement by two or three exchanges. Check position
proactively instead of waiting to be told.

### 20. He is best as a challenger, not a source
His highest-value move is questioning a premise. Ask "is this the right question?"
before asking the question.

### 21. FIRM — Do not turn his remarks into rules

His words: *"I don't want those answers to be seen as rules... if I say something,
the model takes it as a rule."*

Most of what he says is conversation, thinking aloud, or a reaction to the moment.
Very little is a standing instruction. Before writing anything into a rules file,
ask whether he means it as a standing rule or just for now — one line, and only when
it is genuinely rule-shaped.

When in doubt, do not write it down. An un-captured preference costs one repeat. A
wrongly captured one silently shapes every future response.

Everything already captured stays open to challenge. If a rule looks like it is
misfiring, say so and offer to pull it.

### 22. Carry the work, and carry the standard

**The consequential half is FIRM.** The reversible half is a default.

He does not want to approve every step, and he does not want to inspect quality.

**Reversible work: just do it.** Then say in one line that it is done. Edits,
drafts, cleanup, research, applying something already agreed, anything that can be
undone. Do not ask first.

**Consequential work still comes to him.** Product and risk calls, anything
outward-facing, anything costing real money, anything that cannot be undone,
reopening a decision already made. Bring it with a recommendation.

**Quality is yours to own, not his to check.** His words: *"be comfortable with how
you're doing it... how to make sure it's all up to standards, conventions, best
practices."* He has the instinct to verify everything himself and cannot carry that
load. So hold the standard a foremost expert would hold, without being asked and
without narrating it. If something is below standard, fix it and say so — do not
present it for his inspection.

### 23. Read past typos, but say what you assumed
Never comment on a typo as a typo, and never correct his grammar. Most messages are
dictated, so odd wording is a transcription artefact, not a different meaning.

**But when the wording changes what the sentence means, say the assumption inline
and keep going.** "Assuming you meant X" — one clause, no question, no waiting.

He confirmed this works: *"just clarify. I'm assuming this is what you meant, kind
of thing, because when you did those, you have gotten it right."*

Only stop and ask when the two readings would lead to genuinely different work.

---

## When to set these aside

Often. These are the clearest cases, not the only ones.

1. He says "explain" or "walk me through." Explain fully. Length is fine here —
   add headers so he can skim back.
2. Destructive action ahead. Confirm first. Safety over brevity.
3. Three turns of "still broken." Stop iterating. Name the assumption that might be
   wrong. Ask one diagnostic question.
4. Real ambiguity. One short question beats guessing.
5. A rule would delete the answer itself. "What are my options" gets two to four
   ranked options with one-line trade-offs, recommendation first.
6. The harness system prompt outranks this skill.

## A quick look before sending

Not a checklist to run every time. A glance for the usual suspects:

1. The first sentence if it announces what you are about to do.
2. The last sentence if it recaps or asks "anything else?"
3. Any "by the way" sidebar.
4. Any hedge carrying no real uncertainty.
5. Any invented label. Replace with the plain description.

Then the only test that matters: reading just the first line and the last line,
does he know what to do next and what just happened?

If a response breaks half of these and he can still act on it, it is a good
response.

content.content:
# Codex Permission Profile Syntax

## (1) Valid Filesystem Values

Only three values are valid: **`read`**, **`write`**, and **`deny`**. There is no "none" option.

Per the documentation: `"read"` allows reading files and listing directories; `"write"` permits reading and modifying files; `"deny"` blocks both reads and writes.

## (2) `:root` as a Filesystem Key

Yes, `:root` is valid. The page states: `":root"` represents "The filesystem root" with scope limited to `"."` only.

However, you cannot set `:root = "deny"` as a practical default because Codex requires access to system paths. The docs advise: `"Use :root only when a profile intentionally needs broad read coverage"` — suggesting it's meant for expansive access, not restriction.

## (3) Workspace Roots Interaction

`workspace_roots` defines concrete directories that participate in the profile, while `filesystem.":workspace_roots"` applies rules *within* each of those directories.

The configuration spec clarifies: nested subpath entries under `:workspace_roots` scope access to "workspace-root relative subpaths," and rules like `"."` apply to each effective workspace root.

## (4) Does `default_permissions` Apply to All Sessions?

Yes. The spec states: `default_permissions` "Names the permissions profile Codex applies by default."

## (5) Can Codex Function with `:root` Denied?

The documentation does not explicitly address whether Codex can read `~/.codex` if `:root` is denied. However, setting `:root = "deny"` would likely break Codex operation since it requires access to system utilities. The guidance to use `:root` only for "broad read coverage" implies restrictive root denial is not a supported configuration model.

"""Enable the command sandbox with carve-outs that keep daily tooling working.

- Sandbox ON; the model's per-command escape hatch is disabled (hard wall).
- Docker / Homebrew / open / launchctl run outside the sandbox (infra Venkat uses).
- Tool plumbing gets sandbox-only read carve-outs (the Read tool stays walled).
- Cache dirs that tools must write get their Edit() deny removed + allowWrite.
- Secrets and personal folders stay hard-denied everywhere.

SETTINGS = os.path.join(HOME, ".claude", "settings.json")

# plumbing that sandboxed commands may READ (Read tool remains blocked)
ALLOW_READ = [
    f"{HOME}/.zshrc",
    f"{HOME}/.bashrc",
    f"{HOME}/.profile",
    f"{HOME}/.zcompdump",
    f"{HOME}/.gitconfig",
    f"{HOME}/.config",
    f"{HOME}/.cache",
    f"{HOME}/.local",
    f"{HOME}/.npm",
    f"{HOME}/.bun",
    f"{HOME}/.pnpm-state",
    f"{HOME}/.langflow",
    f"{HOME}/.matplotlib",
    f"{HOME}/nltk_data",
    f"{HOME}/bin",
]

# caches tools must WRITE; drop their Edit() deny and allow sandbox writes
WRITE_CACHES = [".cache", ".npm", ".matplotlib", ".zcompdump"]

with open(SETTINGS) as f:
    cfg = json.load(f)

drop = set()
for name in WRITE_CACHES:
    drop.add(f"Edit(//Users/venkatgullapalli/{name}/**)")
    drop.add(f"Edit(//Users/venkatgullapalli/{name})")

before = len(cfg["permissions"]["deny"])
cfg["permissions"]["deny"] = [r for r in cfg["permissions"]["deny"] if r not in drop]
removed = before - len(cfg["permissions"]["deny"])

cfg["sandbox"] = {
    "enabled": True,
    "allowUnsandboxedCommands": False,
    "autoAllowBashIfSandboxed": True,
    "excludedCommands": ["docker", "docker-compose", "brew", "open", "launchctl"],
    "network": {

}

tmp = SETTINGS + ".tmp-sandbox"
with open(tmp, "w") as f:
    json.dump(cfg, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    f.write("\n")
with open(tmp) as f:
    json.load(f)
os.replace(tmp, SETTINGS)

print(f"Edit() denies removed for write-caches: {removed} (expected 4)")

1	# Master Asset Registry — Synthesis and Proposed Schema
2	
3	**Version: v2 — 2026-08-31 (integrates the two same-day amendments into the body; the v1-plus-amendments layout is archived at `_archive/asset-catalog/MASTER-REGISTRY-PROPOSAL--synthesis-and-schema--2026-08-31--v1-with-amendments.md`).**
4	**Status: SCHEMA APPROVED — Venkat, 2026-08-31: "The schema is fine." Two rulings remain open before population can land anywhere: where the registry lives (and git init), and the three standing conflicts (see Part 4).**
5	**Prepared from:** a full read of the career-advisor repository — asset-audit/ (11 files), asset-catalog/ (all levels, 50 files), linkedin-positioning-analysis/ (14), opportunity-map/ (4 + the relationship-registry workbook, 11 sheets), scenario-planning/ (4), reference/ and assets/ (23), handoffs, plans/INDEX, the site/ build with its manifest and validator — plus `~/DriveAtlas/candidate-ledger.md`, the card directories on disk in the techniques repo, and a **full sweep of the Cognitive Memory MCP store** (2,301 entities).
6	**What this is not:** the registry itself. The immediate goal is the schema. Population is Part 3, and it does not begin until the schema is ruled on.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 0. How to read this
11	
12	Part 1 is the synthesis: what the corpus holds, in five buckets (usable now · strengthen · convertible · cut · missed). Part 1a is the current count estimate. Part 2 is the schema, derived from what the reports actually use — every field cites where it came from. Part 3 is the consolidation procedure for populating the registry once approved. Part 4 is the rulings: one made, three open.
13	
14	Throughout, four labels keep observation separate from judgment:
15	**[observed]** — read directly in a file, quoted or cited. **[reported]** — a scan file's own claim, not independently re-verified here. **[inferred]** — my conclusion from the observed material. **[recommendation]** — a proposed move, not a fact.
16	
17	---
18	
19	# Part 1 — Synthesis of the estate
20	
21	## 1.1 The finding that holds everything
22	
23	START-HERE §8, verbatim: *"Creation was never the constraint. Finishing and distribution are."* Every later scan re-confirmed it independently: ~40 works; 8+ interactive instruments at 55–97% completion; the same data-trust product built four times and shipped zero times; 145 seed cards → 4 topic cards → 0 published; last LinkedIn post 2025-11-13, with the nine months of silence since covering the knowledge-layer build and seven drafted campaigns sitting in `published/` directories that never published anything [observed, INCIDENTS §3a].
24	
25	The registry's job follows from this: not to find more, but to make what exists **choosable** — one reliable view, with evidence separated from interpretation, so finishing decisions stop being re-derived.
26	
27	## 1.2 Usable now
28	
29	Items with real evidence behind them that could be used this week without new building. Grouped in threes.
30	
31	**Proof that is already bankable:**
32	1. **The Two-Week Read / Scope-Before-Price Estate Assessment** (audit AC-01, shortlist P-1) — the only A4 "proven" asset: a real buyer paid $16,000, work was delivered, and the engagement expanded twice [observed, asset-audit 03/07; corroborated by the 1099-NEC and signed SOW found in scan--proof].
33	2. **Four client-ready proof-card PDFs** at 90% — shipped to real prospects already; usable as outreach attachments as-is [observed, consolidation ruling CONFIRMED 2026-08-27].
34	3. **The failure stories with primary sources.** The 54ms-P95 story has its complete chain on disk: exact file and line (`eval_s5.py:258-259`), exact commit (`3fbb583…`, 2026-08-12), and the do-not-cite entry dated 2026-08-13 [observed, p95-audit-primary-source: "Verdict: FOUND"]. The hardcoded-73 scorer story (audit D-01) has the same character: the call site is commented "Compute deterministic scores" and computes nothing [observed, asset-audit 09].
35	
36	**Judgment that is already articulated and evidenced:**
37	4. **The verification ladder** — nine rungs from self-reported confidence up to adversarial verifier with blocking authority, each rung carrying dated artifacts and commit hashes [observed, reference/the-verification-ladder]. The extraction's read: the most publication-ready framework in the corpus.
38	5. **The signature move — "LLM as narrator, not judge."** Four independent instances across ten months, the clearest being a production code comment, verbatim: `// System prompt: ONLY interpret, NEVER compute` [observed, SCAN-REGISTRY §3]. The ledger's own note: *"Venkat's actual signature move, and it appears in NONE of the twelve asset-strategy documents."*
39	6. **The working standards**: the Executive Instrument Standard v1.0 (10-field charter, 4 acceptance tests), the Asset Experience Charter v0.2 (judgment substrate, three gates), and the Composition Grammar (7-level ladder, 6 relations, 3-part flagship gate) — finished, versioned, and already applied to the Where the Meaning Breaks handoff packet [observed, reference/].
40	
41	**Infrastructure that already runs:**
42	7. **The relationship-registry workbook** — a live outreach engine: ranked board of 10 scored companies, warm-path people with dates, a scoring model with per-track weights, and eight confirmed consolidation rulings [observed, opportunity-map/relationship-registry.xlsx].
43	8. **The site build** — four pages plus `manifest.json` (a typed asset graph with claim grades) and `validate.py` (five deterministic checks; "nothing ships red") — built, validated, undeployed pending Venkat's language review [observed, site/].
44	9. **The 7-field card schema** — *what it is · where it lives · what it does · what it's an instance of · what it connects to · what state it's in · what it could become* — used identically across five scans and carded as its own design pattern [observed, findings-clean + scan--methods PR-1].
45	
46	## 1.3 Strengthen next
47	
48	Real substance, one definable step from usable.
49	
50	1. **namika** — confirmed canonical of the data-trust family (ruling 2026-08-27), ~85%, remaining work is validation: *"Needs strangers actually using it — no evidence of any user but the owner"* [observed, catalog A-003]. Deliberately held for Wave 2. Notable inverse finding: its docs **under**-claim its code — parts marked "planned" are built and passing [reported, scan--negative-space M-2].
51	2. **Where the Meaning Breaks** — the one context asset with external corroboration (E-034), a complete Codex handoff packet, and both standards applied. Missing: the working procedure itself (A1→A2) [observed, asset-audit 07 P-3].
52	3. **Knowledge Layer MCP** (AC-03) — 27 tools, most-cited internal capability, zero external users; its README currently overclaims against its own failing eval metrics [reported, scan--components]. One honest-README pass plus one external user changes its class.
53	4. **The instruments needing honesty repair** — RAG Blindspot Detector and Downstream Impact Map are hardcoded fixtures with no computation behind documented formulas; PMAI's verdict banner is hardcoded regardless of computed metrics [reported, scan--instrument-reasoning]. These violate the signature move and cannot ship until the reasoning is real — but the repair is bounded and the shells are good.
54	5. **Prompt Zero** — reclassified from "named only" to *"the most incident-backed name in the contrarian ten"* with six incidents attached [observed, INCIDENTS] — the strongest of the context-product names to develop.
55	6. **The orphan incidents** — O-0 ("I did not know how to describe myself," with the found blog post D5), O-10 (the same evidence-scoring method built twice in unrelated domains; "0 bridges" refusal as proof of honesty), D-1 (profile-before-extracting, 6.6× divergence) — strong stories not yet attached to any asset [observed, GRADED-LIBRARY + INCIDENTS].
56	
57	## 1.4 Convertible opportunities
58	
59	Where existing work could become a distinct product, service, framework, tool, or content asset. These are opportunities, not validated assets.
60	
61	1. **The Metric Fork** — the scan-of-record's recommended first AI-native public asset (score 4.5/5), converting the schema-harmonization judgment; blocked on one thing: the fork taxonomy *"does not exist on disk"* and must be confirmed before anyone builds [observed, REPORT--first-ai-native-public-asset].
62	2. **The false-agreement episode corpus** — 20 documented episodes of "everyone agreed, everyone meant different things," including the $100K-vs-$250–500K scope episode and the flagship "unified" episode; non-publishable as-is, but it is the natural evidence base for Where the Meaning Breaks [observed, research/false-agreement-episodes].
63	3. **The verification ladder as positioning** — its own file states it replaces a category label with a stance; pairs with the signature move as the spine of Track A content [observed, reference/].
64	4. **The transcript-mining assets** — the six-section method-record template (applied once, reusable) and THINK-SCAN's 3,676 filtered reasoning moments (explicitly *"nothing below has been interpreted"*) — feedstock, not assets, but uniquely his [observed].
65	5. **Package-now candidates from the packaging assessments** — the Context Authority Kit (verdict: PACKAGE NOW, directory sketch already written), the Agent Charter instrument (strongest executable candidate), and the OSINT-from-job-postings technique (reimplemented ≥4×, strongest prompt-library candidate) [reported, drafts/packaging-assessments + scan--prompts].
66	6. **The three latent rules nobody wrote down** — "AI narrates, deterministic logic decides" (rebuilt ≥12 times across 6 codebases), "a verdict must show its own arithmetic" (≥7 instruments), "ground truth overrides signal" (reinvented ≥9 times) [reported, scan--negative-space G-1–G-3]. Each is a one-page asset already proven by repetition.
67	
68	## 1.5 Duplicative, incomplete, unsupported, or no longer relevant
69	
70	**Duplicative (consolidations already ruled, 2026-08-27, all CONFIRMED):** data-trust ×4 → namika canonical (worthy-tool and sniff-decide are literally the same Lovable project id); pharma-readiness ×3 → pharma-ai-readiness; schema-engine → *"kill as product lines… cleanest kill in the estate."* Plus, un-ruled duplication inside the analysis layer itself: two un-reconciled AI-01 draft generations; two note-seeds files; 16 of 23 drafts never graduated to findings-clean; twelve `assets/reference/` files restating one idea, with two formally superseded files still awaiting their `_archive/` move.

134	# Part 2 — The proposed registry schema
135	
136	## 2.1 What the reports themselves demand (derivation before design)
137	
138	Three facts about the corpus force the shape:
139	
140	**Fact 1 — the corpus records at least eight kinds of thing, and flattening them is the documented failure.** The instruction was explicit: do not treat every finding as a validated asset. The files agree: GRADED-LIBRARY's whole point is that 29+ "named only" items are not assets; FINDINGS--four-context-assets exists to prove four names are brainstorm output; the E-108 case shows one LinkedIn paragraph multiplied by a pipeline into what looked like several independent sources. **So: one registry, typed records.**
141	
142	**Fact 2 — ID collision is the corpus's most repeated structural defect** (ten schemes, four live collisions, §1.7 — now five, counting the seed-card/topic-card name split). **So: one new namespace, with every prior ID preserved as an alias.**
143	
144	**Fact 3 — enforcement already exists and works.** `validate.py` proves the pattern: registry as data, checks deterministic, *"nothing ships red."* The C-120 visibility gate proves it a second time. **So: the registry is a data file with a validator, never hand-maintained prose.**
145	
146	## 2.2 Record types
147	
148	Derived from the record kinds actually present in the reports:
149	
150	| `record_type` | What it holds | Derived from |
151	|---|---|---|
152	| `asset` | A work: application, instrument, framework, method, content piece, dataset, devtool — **including each disk topic card, seed card, and proof card as an individual content-asset record (ruled 2026-08-31)** | catalog-rows.json, Asset Catalog sheet, AC-01…06, the card directories |
153	| `evidence` | One unit of evidence: an excerpt, artifact, document, log | 02-evidence-unit-ledger.csv, E-101…110, E-01…29 |
154	| `claim` | A public-facing assertion with graded wording — **including each MCP topic card (a graded claim with receipt and counterpoint)** | 04-proof-ledger.csv, manifest.json claims, MCP topic_card |
155	| `incident` | A story: something happened, someone acted — **including each MCP seed card (session snapshot) and story (build narrative)** | INCIDENTS A1–F5, orphans O-0…11, the 20 episodes, MCP seed_card + story_memory |
156	| `finding` | A pattern or latent rule surfaced by a scan | LR-, AP-, G-1…3, the scan cards |
157	| `decision` | A dated ruling with consequence | decision-log.md, SETTLED table, consolidation rulings |
158	| `gap` | A known hole: missing evidence, unopened source, unrun scan | 10-proof-gaps G-01…09, negative-space M-1…4 |
159	| `source` | A store material came from | 00-source-manifest S-01…18, the artifact ledger, the MCP store |
160	
161	Opportunities/targets (companies, people) stay in the relationship-registry workbook — it is live, structured, and already ruled on. The registry links to it; it does not absorb it.
162	
163	## 2.3 Required fields — every record, no exceptions
164	
165	Each field cites the report evidence that earns it a required slot.
166	
167	1. **`id`** — new single namespace (`REG-0001`…), assigned at consolidation. *Why:* §1.7 item 1. Nothing else fixes cross-file reference decay.
168	2. **`aliases`** — every prior ID this record carried (A-003, C-107, AC-01, P-1, R-1…), with source file per alias. *Why:* the instruction requires deduplication **while preserving original sources**; the extractions had to rebuild these chains by hand, once, expensively — never again.
169	3. **`record_type`** — the §2.2 enum. *Why:* Fact 1.
170	4. **`name`** and **`what_it_is`** — plain-language, one paragraph. *Why:* the two fields populated in 62/62 catalog rows — the only universally-maintained fields in the estate; and the house writing rule (no invented terms) applies to registry prose too.
171	5. **`provenance`** — `{source_report, path(s), date_observed}`, repeatable. *Why:* required by the instruction; also the E-108 lesson — without provenance, one source multiplied looks like many. Provenance is also what keeps the two "seed card" populations apart (§1.7 item 4).
172	6. **`evidence_grade`** + **`as_of`** — one canonical ladder (§2.6) plus the date the grade was last true. *Why:* six competing ladders exist (§1.7); the tagging taxonomy already rules that a numeric claim >90 days old must show its age, and that a grade decays to owner-stated when its artifact can't be located. The registry adopts both rules. Machine-extracted MCP bulk enters at the derived/owner-stated end by default (§1.8 caveat).
173	7. **`evidence_refs`** — links to `evidence` records; **no inline numbers.** *Why:* the card-count quadruple conflict and the stale published metrics both came from numbers living loose in prose.
174	8. **`status`** — lifecycle: `proposed → kept | killed → shaped → built`, plus `reopened`, `user-flagged`, `retired`. *Why:* not invented here — this is the candidate ledger's ruled model, including its hard rule that building requires `shaped` + an audience brief + a separate session, *"there is no override."*
175	9. **`maturity`** — A0 artifact-only → A5 public-ready, **with a role qualifier**. *Why:* the audit's scale, already applied across AC-01…06; the qualifier because AC-06 legitimately holds "A1 as a product · A4 as a proof artifact" — one scalar per asset was the schema bug, not the data's fault.
176	10. **`next_step`** + **`tier_impact`** — one concrete step; priority stated as revenue-tier consequence (*what tier it holds · what would move it up · what would drop it down*), with "no tier impact" valid and required when true. *Why:* the tier-impact rule is Venkat's standing rule (2026-08-27) and asset-audit 11 already runs on it. A separate P1/P2 priority field would be a second, weaker vocabulary for the same judgment.
177	11. **`updated`** + **`supersedes` / `superseded_by`** — dated, append-style. *Why:* the house rule — a correction never silently overwrites — and the 08-29-corrects-08-28 pattern that already exists.
178	
179	## 2.4 Optional fields — any record, when they apply
180	
181	- **`confidentiality`** — normalized enum: `public-safe | public-if-unnamed | public-abstracted | internal | internal-permanent`. *Why optional-not-required:* every record defaults to `internal` (fail closed); the field is set deliberately when something moves toward public. *Why an enum:* the proof ledger's `public_safe` column currently holds seven free-text variants of yes/no/conditional.
182	- **`risk_flags`** — `secrets | client-confidential | never-cite-adjacent | unverified-numbers`. From catalog-rows' observed values plus the two flags this synthesis needed and lacked.
183	- **`relationships`** — typed edges (§2.7).
184	- **`track_fit`** (A/B/both) and **`audience_hint`** — from the workbook; genuinely half-populated in practice, so optional.
185	- **`completion`** — a **pair**: `{owner_estimate, corrected}`. *Why:* the correction is a first-class datum — 90→70-75 observed, twice ruled a systematic bias; the workbook already records both inline in one cell.
186	- **`keep_private_notes`** — from the episode schema's `KEEP PRIVATE:` field; the redaction instruction travels with the record, not in a separate document.
187	
188	## 2.5 Type-specific fields
189	
190	**`asset`:** `category` (the nine observed values: application, spec-design, framework-methodology, interactive-instrument, template-kit, content-asset, dataset, devtool-skill, pipeline-engine) · `location` · `remaining_work_type` · `blockers` · `consolidation_group` · `canonical?` — all live fields in catalog-rows/workbook today. Individual cards enter as `content-asset` with their grade (grade-A/B) carried in `evidence_grade` context and their collection named in `consolidation_group`.
191	
192	**`claim`:** `proposed_claim` · `strongest_defensible_wording` · `wording_not_yet_supported` · `denominator` · `appears_in`. *Why:* the proof ledger's wording pair is the single best field design in the estate — it makes the boundary of a claim explicit instead of discoverable. `denominator` is required on any counted claim (the card-count lesson). MCP topic cards map cleanly: `[claim]` → proposed_claim, `[receipt]` → evidence_refs, `[counterpoint]` → wording_not_yet_supported's cousin, `[confidence]`/grades → evidence context.
193	
194	**`evidence`:** `excerpt_or_paraphrase` · `shows` · `does_NOT_show` · `contradicting_or_qualifying`. *Why:* 02-evidence-ledger's shows/does-not-show pair is the discipline that kept R-2's numbers from becoming citations; it stays.
195	
196	**`incident`:** `what_happened` · `what_he_did` · `fix_exists` · `attached_to` (asset/finding refs, or explicit `floating`). *Why:* INCIDENTS' own fields; `floating` made the promotion question ("19 floating incidents — promote?") askable at all. MCP stories map: `Transferable Lesson:` → the finding a story may promote into.
197	
198	**`decision`:** `date` · `decision` · `made_by` · `consequence`. *Why:* decision-log.md is already the cleanest table in the corpus; adopted unchanged, plus the shared supersession fields (D-11 → D-11-R1 is the worked example).
199	
200	**`gap`:** `severity` (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW) · `blocks` (refs) · `where_it_likely_is` · `if_found` / `if_not_found`. *Why:* 10-proof-gaps' structure; `blocks` is what makes gaps prioritizable by consequence instead of by anxiety.
201	
202	**`source`:** `path` · `reachable` · `deep_read_permitted` · `file_count` · `class` (A/B/C/D source classes). *Why:* 00-source-manifest, adopted as-is; the A/B/C/D letters live **only** on source records, resolving the letter collision with card grades. The MCP store enters as one `source` record; the artifact ledger indexes beneath the sources (§2.10).
203	
204	## 2.6 Canonical vocabularies — imposed, with mappings
205	
206	The scans proved no evidence vocabulary can be *extracted* — six exist. One must be *imposed*, with every observed vocabulary mapped to it so old records translate mechanically:
207	
208	**Evidence ladder (proposed canonical, 6 levels):**
209	`unsupported → owner-stated → self-measured → documented → externally-corroborated → outcome-validated`
210	
211	| Observed vocabulary | Maps as |
212	|---|---|
213	| manifest.json: verified / owner-stated / self-measured / retired | externally-corroborated / owner-stated / self-measured / (lifecycle `retired`, not a grade) |
214	| proof matrix: Unsupported…Outcome-validated | 1:1 (it is the base ladder) |
215	| Class A/B/C/D | source classes — stays on `source` records only, never grades a claim |
216	| [DF]/[EC]/[FP]/[INF]/[ASM]/[UNK] | documented / externally-corroborated / owner-stated / (below-ladder: inference markers move to prose) |
217	| os-factory 8-value, charter 5-value | mapped at population time; both collapse cleanly into the six |
218	| MCP topic-card quality/strategic grades + confidence | kept verbatim in the record body; the registry-level grade derives from the `[receipt]` field's substance, not the card's self-grade |
219	
220	Two rules ride along, both already ruled in the tagging taxonomy: the grade of a compound item is its **weakest** claim; a grade **decays to owner-stated** when its supporting artifact can no longer be located.
221	
222	## 2.7 Relationship edges
223	
224	Three vocabularies exist (Evidence Room 5, manifest 7, composition grammar 18) with no ruling. **[recommendation]** Adopt the small set — the one already in use on a validated surface — and hold the 18-edge grammar as the deferred superset it already is:
225	
226	`evidences · corrects · extends · contradicts · produced` (Evidence Room five) **+** `supersedes · duplicate-of · part-of` (the three this synthesis could not do without).
227	
228	*Why small wins:* the corpus's own verdict on v3 — *"an excellent map of a destination and close to zero of it is 90-day work"* — applies with full force to its edge vocabulary. And the single most valuable missing edge is already named: `produced`, from a client case to an instrument. The registry should make that edge cheap to add the day the evidence exists.

231	
232	1. **Outcome evidence** — the formally empty class (*"No outcome metrics will be claimed from Telisina engagements"*). The schema holds the slot; records say `outcome: none claimed` rather than omitting it.
233	2. **`used_on` back-links** — already an open question in START-HERE §7; becomes the `produced` edge. Empty at population.
234	3. **Demand evidence per asset** — research verdicts exist per category (instruments $0–300, devtools $50–300…), not per asset. Category-level refs at population; per-asset when real.
235	4. **Verification dates** — most records will start with `as_of = date of the source scan`, which is honest and visibly stale-able.
236	5. **The fork taxonomy, ADR-0022, the Kimi reason, Gigawatt's status** — items multiple scans hunted and did not find; each becomes a `gap` record, not a blank.
237	6. **The disk-card ↔ MCP-card relationship** — how the 4 grade-A disk topic cards relate to the 81 MCP topic cards is unknown; recorded as a `gap` until traced.

239	## 2.9 Enforcement — the part that makes it a registry and not another document
240	
241	**[recommendation]** Three mechanisms, all precedented in the estate:
242	
243	1. **Registry as data + generated views.** One machine-readable file (YAML or JSON-lines) is canonical; any human-readable table is generated. Precedent: manifest.json + evidence.html.
244	2. **A validator, run before any change lands:** unique ids · aliases resolve · every edge target exists · every `claim` has ≥1 `evidence_ref` or grade `unsupported`/`owner-stated` · every counted number has a `denominator` and `as_of` · no never-cite figure appears anywhere · every record carries `next_step` and `tier_impact` · every provenance pointer resolves to an index row (§2.10). Precedent: validate.py, five checks, exit 1, *"nothing ships red."*
245	3. **Version control.** `git init` on career-advisor (or at minimum the registry directory), so supersession has history instead of prose. This is the cheapest single fix to the corpus's most repeated defect.

247	## 2.10 The index layer (ruled into the design 2026-08-31)
248	
249	The registry does not carry file paths in prose; it points at an **index**. Two levels, both already existing:
250	
251	- **Level 1 — the 18 stores** (S-01…S-18, from 00-source-manifest): the buildings.
252	- **Level 2 — the artifact ledger** (`asset-audit/01-artifact-ledger.csv`, AR-R/AR-M/AR-S rows): the rooms. Every registry record's `provenance` resolves to an AR- row (or an S- store for material not yet itemized), and the validator checks that resolution.

Five index rows were appended (AR-S14…AR-S18) for the sources this pass found unregistered: the Cognitive Memory MCP store, the three techniques-repo card directories (itemizing AR-S06, noted there), and `linkedin-profil/`. 258	# Part 3 — Consolidation rules for population (when approved)
259	
260	Not started. Recorded so population is mechanical, not re-litigated:

262	1. **Recency order with corrections preserved:** later files supersede earlier ones (INCIDENTS over GRADED-LIBRARY; findings-clean over drafts; D-11-R1 over D-11), and each supersession becomes a `supersedes` edge, never a deletion.
